transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Stocks opened mixed after the Labor Department reported a bigger than expected jump in wholesale
prices last month.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose more than 160 points
in early trading.
Retail inflation was high in September, but wholesale inflation was even higher.
Prices at the wholesale level jumped 1.3 percent between August and September, the biggest
one-month increase in more than four years.
Despite rising prices, shoppers continued to spend freely last month.
Retail spending rose by eight-tenths of a percentage point in September, which is more
than forecasters expected.
Much of that extra spending went for pricey gasoline, but people also spent more at restaurants
and grocery stores.
Meanwhile, spending was down in September at home improvement centers.
The Federal Reserve will consider both the inflation data and the robust spending when
policymakers meet to talk about interest rates later this month.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
A federal judge in California has halted the Trump administration's controversial reorganization
of the Agriculture Department.
And Piers Kirk Seigler reports on the ruling that also stopped the relocation of the U.S.
Forest Service for now.
The Trump administration has planned to close or consolidate dozens of federal research stations,
primarily in the northwest, and move the headquarters of the U.S. Forest Service from Washington,
D.C. to Utah.
That's ignited particular controversy due to the fact that Utah has more desert lands
than forests and is on the forefront of an effort by conservative western states to take
over control of federal public lands.
The judge in the case brought by federal employee unions wrote that this broader reorganization
can't be done without the consent and funding of Congress.
The judge gave the administration two days to respond to most of the order but broadly
halted the USDA reorganization.
Trump officials have said it's needed to modernize and make the agency more efficient while unions
and conservationists are likening it to a dismantling.
Kirk Seigler, NPR News.
A major source of fraud in the federal food assistance program called SNAP has to do with
its outdated security features.
Hundreds of millions of dollars have been stolen from SNAP recipients.
NPR's Julianna Kim reports Congress is now considering upgrading the tech.
In most states, food assistance cards rely on swipe pay with magnetic stripes, leaving
them extremely vulnerable to a type of fraud known as card skimming.
Democratic Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon has been pushing for cards to have microchips,
which is the standard for most debit and credit cards today.
We've been hearing the Republicans talk about rooting out waste, fraud, and abuse in hunger
programs.
My bill gives you a way to do it without taking food away from hungry children.
The Senate version of the farm bill includes a provision to roll out chips, but the House
version does not, meaning it's unclear if the measure will make the final cut.
Julianna Kim, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR.
Ukraine says it's going to start attacking Russian oil refineries again.
President Trump told Ukraine not to do this.
Trump also claimed that Russia had agreed to a cease-fire on striking energy targets,
but Russia never stopped firing.
Ukraine's president says his country briefly held off, but is resuming strikes.
Hitting the energy targets can help Ukraine degrade Russia's ability to sell oil internationally.
More than 9,000 people have gotten sick from the ongoing Ebola outbreak.
NPR's Jonathan Lambert reports cases are popping up outside the epicenter.
Democratic Republic of Congo officials confirmed that there have been 9,144 cases and over
4,400 deaths, making this the second largest Ebola outbreak ever.
Early hotspots of spread have slowed down a bit, but the virus has moved into new territory.
The province of North Kivu is particularly affected.
An ongoing conflict there is slowing response efforts.
Over 70 percent of deaths are still occurring outside of treatment centers.
That suggests efforts to monitor potential cases and get them to seek treatment are falling
short.
The virus is also spreading outside of DRC.
Last week, Kenya reported its first case in a man who traveled home from DRC.
Now one of his family members has gotten sick.
Kenyan health officials said this second case was already in quarantine and is now being
treated.
Jonathan Lambert, NPR News.
Online streamer Netflix says it will lay off about 6 percent of its work force.
That's about 1,000 positions.
It's one of Netflix's biggest layoffs in years.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Stocks open mixed after wholesale prices jump 1.3 percent in September, the biggest monthly rise in four years
Retail spending rises 0.8 percent in September, with gasoline, restaurants, and grocery stores driving gains
Federal judge in California halts Trump administration's reorganization of the Agriculture Department and Forest Service relocation to Utah
Senate and House farm bills differ on whether SNAP food assistance cards will get microchips to combat skimming fraud
Ukraine says it will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries despite Trump's request to hold off
Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo reaches 9,144 cases and over 4,400 deaths, spreading to new areas
Kenya's second Ebola case confirmed, a family member of the first patient who traveled home from Congo
Netflix to lay off about 6 percent of its workforce, roughly 1,000 positions, one of its biggest cuts in years
